title: Family Columns
description: Ten warm, reflective columns by different writers on family life: a teenager learning to cook, video calls with grandparents, a recipe box, two sisters in one room, a dog in charge, a first day at college, a reunion in the rain, an old photo album, a blackout and a season of hockey.

lessons.title: Teaching Leo to Cook
lessons.summary: A mother teaches her teenage son to cook, one evening a week, until he cooks rice for a friend.
lessons.text:
When my son Leo turned fifteen, I made a decision that I am still proud of: before he left home, he would know how to feed himself. He did not share my enthusiasm. He frowned at the idea, the way teenagers frown at most ideas that come from their parents, but he agreed to give me one evening a week.

We began with rice, because rice seems simple until you try to cook it. I chose jasmine rice, a rice from Thailand with long grains and a soft smell of flowers. Leo asked why we could not just use the rice that comes in a bag for the microwave. I told him that jasmine rice cooked properly in a pot is one of life's small pleasures.

The first lesson was about patience. Leo wanted to lift the lid every two minutes to see what was happening. Each time he did, the steam escaped, and in the end the rice was hard in the middle and burned at the bottom. He looked into the pot and declared himself completely incompetent. I told him that nobody is incompetent after one try; they are simply new.

The second week we made a tomato sauce, and the teaspoon became his enemy. The recipe asked for one teaspoon of salt. Leo was in a hurry. He fumbled with the lid of the salt jar, fumbled again with the spoon, and used a large tablespoon instead of the teaspoon. We tasted the sauce together. It was like drinking the sea.

By the fourth week, he wanted to cook seafood. His grandfather had been a fisherman, and Leo had grown up eating shrimp and fish at his house. We bought shrimp and a piece of white fish, and we also made black beans, which had to stay in water overnight. In the morning, the beans had soaked up so much water that they had doubled in size, and Leo, who had never seen soaked beans before, was impressed in spite of himself.

His first attempt to fry the fish was less successful. He put far too much oil in the pan, and by the end the paper towels under the fish were saturated with oil, so saturated that they fell apart in his hands. The whole kitchen smelled of seafood for two days.

The real reward came a month later. A friend of Leo's stayed for dinner, and Leo said casually, "I'll make the rice." He said it casually, as if he had been doing it all his life, and I pretended to read a magazine. He did not lift the lid once. The jasmine rice was perfect. When his friend asked for more, Leo frowned at the compliment, the way he frowns at everything, but I could see that he was pleased.

Questions:
What went wrong the first time Leo cooked rice?
He lifted the lid too often, so the steam escaped and the rice was hard in the middle and burned at the bottom.
What mistake did Leo make with the salt?
He fumbled with the jar and the spoon and used a tablespoon instead of a teaspoon.
What happened to the paper towels under the fish?
They were saturated with oil, so they fell apart in his hands.
How did Leo offer to make the rice for his friend?
He said it casually, as if he had been doing it all his life.

lessons.title: Granny on the Screen
lessons.summary: A father describes his parents' Sunday video calls with his children, with all their technical troubles.
lessons.text:
Every Sunday at five o'clock, my children's grandparents appear on our kitchen table. They live 1,200 miles away, in a small town in Vermont, and for most of the year the only way we see them is through the tablet that leans against the fruit bowl.

My mother insists that the children call her Granny. She says that Grandma sounds like someone who knits in a rocking chair, while Granny sounds like someone who might still climb a tree. My father is simply Grandpa. He has worn a large gray mustache for fifty years, and on a small screen the mustache is often the first thing we see, because Grandpa holds the tablet too close to his face.

The calls rarely start smoothly. My parents' computer is ten years old, which in the world of technology makes it nearly obsolete. Grandpa says that he is nearly obsolete, too, but that he still works if you are patient with him. There is always a glitch of some kind. Sometimes the picture freezes with Granny's mouth half open. Sometimes the sound arrives two seconds after the picture, so that Grandpa seems to laugh before the joke. The best glitch is a strange distortion that makes their faces long and thin, and our youngest, Ivy, who is six, finds this distortion the funniest thing on Earth.

When the picture is fuzzy, which is most of the time, the children wave anyway. A fuzzy Granny is still Granny.

There is another difficulty. Grandpa has a hearing impairment, and although his hearing aids are excellent, they do not always cooperate with the tablet. The children have learned to speak slowly and to face the screen, and they no longer find his impairment strange. Ivy once explained to a friend that Grandpa hears with his eyes as well as his ears, which is not a bad description of reading lips.

My parents are not as outdated as they like to pretend. Granny has learned to search the internet, although she types her questions as complete, polite sentences instead of a single keyword. When I told her that one keyword, such as "pie" or "weather," was enough, she said that it seemed rude to ask the computer for something without saying please. Her methods may be outdated, but she always finds what she is looking for.

What the children love most is watching their grandparents flirt. After fifty years of marriage, Grandpa still flirts with Granny on every call. He tells the children that she was the most beautiful girl at the county fair, and Granny rolls her eyes and tells him to stop. Then she flirts back by saying that his mustache was the only reason she agreed to dance with him.

The computer may be old and the picture may be fuzzy, but every Sunday at five o'clock, the most important thing comes through perfectly clearly.

Questions:
What does Ivy think of the distortion that makes their faces long and thin?
She finds the distortion the funniest thing on Earth.
How have the children learned to talk to Grandpa?
Because of his hearing impairment, they speak slowly and face the screen.
How does Granny search the internet?
She types complete, polite sentences instead of a single keyword.
How does Granny flirt back with Grandpa?
She says that his mustache was the only reason she agreed to dance with him.

lessons.title: The Recipe Box
lessons.summary: A woman inherits her family's recipe box and learns that one recipe should not be changed.
lessons.text:
When my aunt Ruth moved into a smaller apartment last spring, she gave me the family recipe box. It is a small wooden box with a broken hinge, and it holds about two hundred cards written by three generations of women in my family. In our family you do not buy a recipe box; you inherit one, and I was surprised and honored to inherit this one.

The oldest cards were written by my great-grandmother, Hattie, in brown ink. Her writing is careful and formal, and she never used a contraction. Where I would write "don't stir," she wrote "do not stir." My grandmother's cards, written in blue pen, use a contraction in almost every line, and my mother's cards have contractions and smiling faces.

Some instructions are redundant. One card says, "Add a little salt. Do not forget the salt." Another tells the cook to "heat the oven before you turn it on," which is both redundant and slightly impossible. I love these redundant lines, because I can hear the women who wrote them, worried that someone would forget the important part.

The card that everyone wants is Hattie's bread pudding. It is the most versatile recipe in the box. It needs only old bread, milk, eggs and sugar, and you can add almost anything to it: apples, chocolate or nuts. Hattie made her pudding with whatever was left in the kitchen, and because the recipe was so versatile, it survived the hard years, when nothing could be wasted.

Last Thanksgiving, I made a mistake. I decided to make the pudding more modern. I used coconut milk and less sugar, and I served it with pride. The backlash was immediate. My brother put down his spoon and asked what I had done to Granny Hattie's pudding. My mother said nothing, which was worse. Even my nephew, who is eight, joined the backlash by asking for "the real one." I learned that some recipes are not really recipes but promises.

Friends sometimes tell me that a recipe box is old-fashioned and that I should take photos of the cards and keep them on my phone. They predict the demise of the paper recipe, just as people once predicted the demise of the paper book. I did take photos, just in case, but I keep the box. A photo does not have the grease stain on the pudding card or the place where Hattie's pen pressed through the paper. Those marks are tangible proof that real hands made these dishes in real kitchens. The card is tangible in a way that a photo can never be.

One day my daughter will inherit the box. I have started adding my own cards for her. On the pudding card, I added one line at the bottom, without a contraction, in honor of Hattie: "Do not change this recipe. I tried."

Questions:
What was special about Hattie's language on the cards?
She never used a contraction; she wrote "do not" instead of "don't."
Why is the bread pudding recipe called versatile?
You can add almost anything to it, and it uses whatever is left in the kitchen.
What happened when the writer changed the pudding?
There was an immediate backlash from her family, who wanted the real one.
Why does the writer keep the paper cards?
The cards are tangible proof that real hands made these dishes.

lessons.title: Two Sisters, One Room
lessons.summary: Two sisters who must share a bedroom write their own rules and grow closer.
lessons.text:
When we moved to a smaller house two years ago, our daughters had to share a bedroom. Nora was thirteen and Tess was ten, and they took the news as if we had announced the end of civilization.

The first weeks were hard. Nora found her little sister immature. Tess sang in bed, left her socks on Nora's side of the room and laughed at her own jokes before she had finished telling them. Tess, in turn, said that being serious all the time was just another way of being immature. They argued about trivial things: who had the better pillow, whose turn it was to close the window, whether a sock counts as being on your side if only its toe crosses the line. The arguments were trivial, but to them every one was a war.

My husband's first solution was a wall. He built a low wall down the middle of the room out of plywood, and he fixed a long plank of pine along the top as a shelf, so that each girl had a place for her books. The plywood wall lasted four days as a wall. The girls covered their sides with posters, then they began to pass notes over it, and then Tess discovered that she could sit on her bed, rest her elbows on the plank and talk to her sister for hours. The wall that was supposed to separate them brought them closer.

Soon after, the girls wrote a treaty. I found it taped to the plywood under the title "The Official Agreement of Room 2." It began, "The two people named herein agree to the following rules." Nora had found the word herein in a library book and liked how serious it sounded. The rules herein included no singing after nine, lights out at ten, and one more: any sweater that is borrowed must come with collateral. As collateral, Tess usually offered her favorite stuffed rabbit, which Nora kept on the plank until the sweater came back.

They also had unofficial rules, which were never written down but which everybody knew. The most important unofficial rule was that they could criticize each other, but no one else could. When a girl at school laughed at a drawing of Tess's, Nora told the girl quietly that laughing at a ten-year-old's drawing was pure stupidity. Tess told that story for a month.

There were still bad nights. Sometimes they would wrestle on the floor over a comb, and I would wrestle with my own temper before I went in to separate them and explain the stupidity of fighting over something that cost three dollars.

This fall, Nora will move into the little room upstairs that we have finally finished. She is happy, of course. But last night I heard her ask Tess, over the plywood, whether she could still come back sometimes to talk after lights out. Tess said yes, but only with collateral.

Questions:
Why did Nora and Tess have to share a bedroom?
The family moved to a smaller house.
What did the girls argue about?
They argued about trivial things, such as pillows, the window and socks.
What did the father build, and what happened to it?
He built a plywood wall with a plank on top, and it brought the girls closer instead of separating them.
What did a borrowed sweater need, according to the treaty?
It needed collateral, usually Tess's stuffed rabbit.

lessons.title: The Dog Who Runs Our House
lessons.summary: A large family dog digs, eats what he should not, visits the vet and looks after a little boy.
lessons.text:
Our dog, Bruno, weighs 130 pounds, and he believes that the house belongs to him. He is a heavyweight breed that was once used to pull fishing nets out of the sea and to rescue swimmers. Bruno has never rescued anyone, but he once ate a whole birthday cake, and in our family that counts as a heavyweight achievement.

From Bruno's standpoint, the day has three parts: eating, sleeping and supervising. His daytime routine never changes. In the morning he sleeps in front of the door, so that nobody can leave without stepping over him. In the afternoon he sleeps in the kitchen, in the exact spot where the cook needs to stand. His daytime naps are as loud as an old truck.

When our son, Sam, was born, Bruno appointed himself his nanny. He lay next to the baby's bed for hours, and when Sam cried, Bruno came to find us with a worried face. Sam is seven now, and Bruno still follows him from room to room. He is an honorary member of the family who has, in fact, been here longer than Sam.

He would also like to be an honorary member of the garden club, although the club might not agree. Last spring he began a serious excavation under the apple tree. Each day the hole was bigger, and each day Bruno came inside with a dirty face and a proud expression. My husband filled the hole, and Bruno dug it again. We tried a small fence, but it was ineffective, because Bruno simply lay on it until it fell over. The excavation ended only when he found what he had been looking for: an old tennis ball that Sam had lost two summers before.

This summer he found a less pleasant treasure, a bag of rotten apples behind the shed. He ate most of it, and that night he had terrible diarrhea. We took him to the vet, who looked at him the way a teacher looks at a student who has done something foolish again. She said that the diarrhea would pass in a few days. She decided to prescribe a plain diet of rice and boiled chicken for a week, and a medicine to alleviate the pain in his stomach. "I prescribe this diet to a lot of dogs," she said, "but most of them did not eat the apples on purpose."

The medicine did alleviate the pain, and the diet worked, although Bruno considered it an insult. Every evening he sat by the table and watched us eat with deep sadness. Our attempts to ignore him were completely ineffective.

Now, in the evenings, Sam reads on the living room rug, and Bruno lies beside him like a large, warm sofa. Most nights they both fall asleep there, the boy and his nanny. From my standpoint, it is the best part of the day.

Questions:
Why did Bruno become Sam's nanny?
He lay next to the baby's bed for hours and came to find the parents when Sam cried.
Why was the fence ineffective?
Bruno simply lay on it until it fell over.
How did the excavation under the apple tree end?
It ended when Bruno found an old tennis ball that Sam had lost.
What did the vet prescribe after the rotten apples?
She decided to prescribe a plain diet and a medicine to alleviate the pain.

lessons.title: The Day She Left for College
lessons.summary: Parents drive their daughter to college and wait at home for her first postcard.
lessons.text:
For eighteen years, my daughter Clara has been loud, and our house has been loud with her. Last Saturday we drove her to college, four hours away, and the house has been quiet ever since.

Packing took a week. Clara wanted to bring everything she owned, and I wanted her to bring a warm coat. We agreed on two suitcases and nine cardboard boxes. One suitcase was for clothes. The other suitcase, which she called "essentials," held a lamp, four plants, forty pens and a framed photo of our cat. When I asked about the coat, she said it was in box number six, a cardboard box on which she had written "winter, probably."

We left at six in the morning to avoid the traffic. It was a lovely plan, and it failed. Half the state seemed to be taking a child to college on the same day. The congestion on the highway was so bad that we moved more slowly than a bicycle, and the congestion did not clear until we reached the campus, where every parking space was full. My husband said that the day was going downhill fast, by which he meant that it was getting worse. It also went downhill in a literal sense: Clara's dorm sits at the bottom of a steep hill, so we carried nine boxes downhill and then climbed back up to the car for the suitcases.

Her room was small and bright, and her roommate was friendly. Then it was time to leave. Clara hugged us and promised to send a postcard. I pointed out that nobody sends postcards anymore. She said that was exactly why she would.

The drive home was quiet. I had expected to feel sad, and I did, but I also felt something I had not expected: optimism. College will broaden her world. She will meet people who think differently from us, read books I have never read and broaden her idea of who she might become. My optimism lasted until we got home and I saw her empty room.

The next morning, I began to dispose of the things she had left behind: empty boxes, a broken umbrella, three years of old school papers. Disposing of them felt strange, as if I were putting her childhood away. I kept the drawings.

On Thursday, a postcard arrived. It showed the college library, and on the back Clara had written in large letters: "Classes are hard. Food is bad. Roommate is great. I found the coat." I read it standing in the hall, and I did what any parent would do: I rejoiced. It may seem silly to rejoice over a postcard, but parents learn to rejoice in small things. The postcard is on the refrigerator now, where it will stay until the next one comes.

Questions:
Why did the family move so slowly on the highway?
There was heavy congestion, because half the state was taking a child to college.
In what literal sense did the day go downhill?
Clara's dorm was at the bottom of a steep hill, so they carried the boxes downhill.
Why did the writer feel optimism on the drive home?
She believed that college would broaden her daughter's world.
What did Clara write on her postcard?
She wrote that classes were hard, the food was bad, her roommate was great and she had found the coat.

lessons.title: Rain at the Reunion
lessons.summary: A big family holds its reunion in a park, plays softball and runs from a storm.
lessons.text:
Every two years, my mother's family holds a reunion in Riverside Park, and every two years someone suggests that we rent a hall and hold a proper banquet. The suggestion is always rejected. We are not a banquet family. We are a family of folding tables, paper plates and seventeen kinds of potato salad.

This year, as the oldest cousin, I was in charge of the planning. My uncle Walter, who works in business, called the reunion "a project with many stakeholders," and he was right. Every aunt was a stakeholder with strong opinions about the menu, and every child was a stakeholder with strong opinions about dessert.

The weather forecast was dreadful. It promised heavy rain in the afternoon. My aunt Lucille said that the forecast had been dreadful for the last three reunions and it had never rained once, so we went ahead.

The morning was perfect. After a wet week, the grass was a deep, rich green, almost emerald, and the lake beyond the trees shone like an emerald in the sun. We set up the tables, and about sixty relatives arrived, carrying dishes.

After lunch came the softball game, the most serious event of the day: the cousins against the aunts and uncles. Softball is the gentle cousin of baseball, with a bigger ball and a slower throw, but my family plays it like a world championship. Aunt Lucille, who is 74, hit the ball over the head of the youngest cousin, and we had to stop the game while she walked around the bases to loud applause.

Meanwhile, my cousin Dennis, an amateur magician, entertained the small children. At every reunion he pulls coins from their ears and makes their sandwiches disappear. The greatest trick of any magician, he says, is that the sandwiches never come back. The older children went on a safari through the bushes by the lake, looking for wild animals. Their safari found two frogs, a turtle and a great many ants.

At four o'clock we heard a low rumble from the west. Aunt Lucille said it was a truck. Then came a second rumble, louder, and the sky turned dark gray. Within ten minutes, rain was falling hard. We evacuated the picnic area and ran to the stone pavilion near the parking lot, carrying babies, grandparents and the potato salad. Everybody was evacuated in five minutes, which Uncle Walter called the family's finest hour. We were soaked, but nobody minded.

In the pavilion we held the prize ceremony. For twenty years, the winner of the softball game has stood on an old wooden crate that we call the podium. This year the aunts and uncles won, and Aunt Lucille climbed onto the podium, raised a paper cup of juice and declared it the best reunion yet. Nobody argues with the woman on the podium.

Questions:
Why did Uncle Walter call the reunion a project with many stakeholders?
Every aunt and every child had strong opinions about the food.
What did the children's safari find?
It found two frogs, a turtle and a great many ants.
What did the family do when the rain began?
They evacuated the picnic area and ran to the stone pavilion.
What is the podium?
It is an old wooden crate on which the winner of the softball game stands.

lessons.title: The Album in the Closet
lessons.summary: A woman finds her grandmother's photo album and learns how her great-grandmother came to America.
lessons.text:
Last winter, while I was looking for a lost scarf, I found my grandmother's photo album at the back of the hall closet. It is a heavy book with a cracked leather cover. I sat down on the closet floor to open it and did not get up for two hours.

The first photo shows my great-grandmother, Elsa, at 19, on the day she arrived in New York from Sweden in 1912. She is wearing a dark coat and holding a single suitcase. Her cheeks look strangely dark, and at first I thought the photo was damaged. Then I remembered that rouge often looks dark in old black and white photos. She had put on rouge for her arrival in America, the way you might dress up for a job interview. I like her for that rouge.

Her arrival was not smooth. According to a letter in the album, a clerk wrote her name wrong, and because of the mistake her papers seemed false. For a week she faced the possibility of deportation, of being sent back across the ocean she had just crossed. A friend took her to the Swedish consul, a patient man with round glasses, who wrote a letter confirming who she was. The letter from the consul ended the threat of deportation. Elsa kept it for the rest of her life, and now it is in the album.

She was, she liked to say, a New Yorker for exactly three weeks. Then she took a train to a small town in southeastern Pennsylvania, where she found work as a cook in the house of a parson. The parson had a son named Henry, and two years later Elsa married him. There is a photo of the parson's house: a white house with a tall brick chimney that leans a little to the left. My grandmother used to say that the chimney leaned for a hundred years and never fell, and that the family was the same.

Further on are photos of my grandmother as a girl, of picnics and winters in southeastern Pennsylvania, and one of her in 1951, wearing a maternity dress with a wide white collar, in front of the same leaning chimney. The baby she was expecting in that maternity photo is my mother.

What I noticed most was a square chin, which our family has passed down genetically for five generations. Elsa has it. So does the parson. So do my grandmother and my mother, and so, I noticed with some alarm, do I. My four-year-old daughter already has it, too. Genetically speaking, we are a family of chins.

I carried the album downstairs and showed it to my daughter. She studied Elsa's photo for a long time and asked whether the lady was a New Yorker. I said yes, for three weeks. She said that was enough. We are going to frame the letter from the consul and hang it in the hall.

Questions:
Why do Elsa's cheeks look dark in the photo?
She was wearing rouge, which often looks dark in old black and white photos.
Why did Elsa face the possibility of deportation?
A clerk wrote her name wrong, so her papers seemed false.
Where did Elsa work after New York?
She worked as a cook in the house of a parson in southeastern Pennsylvania.
What has the family inherited genetically?
They have inherited a square chin.

lessons.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
lessons.summary: During a long blackout, a family discovers that storytelling works without electricity.
lessons.text:
My wife, Helen, is a physicist. She studies how liquids move, which means, as she explains to our children, that she thinks about water for a living. Last month she came home from a three-day symposium in Denver, tired and full of new ideas, and an hour later every light on our street went out.

It was the longest blackout we had ever had. A storm had brought down power lines across the county, and the electric company said that the blackout might last until morning. Our children, Owen, who is nine, and Lily, who is six, reacted as if the world had ended. Owen announced that without electricity our family would soon be extinct, like the dinosaurs.

We lit candles and sat together in the living room. At first nobody knew what to do. Then Helen, who had spent three days at the symposium listening to other scientists, decided that it was her turn to talk. She told the children the story of Archimedes, the ancient Greek thinker who, according to legend, noticed that the water in his bath rose when he got in. The rise of the water is called displacement, she explained: a body pushes water out of its way, and the amount of water it moves is equal to the volume of the body under the water. The legend says that Archimedes was so excited by the idea of displacement that he jumped out of the bath and ran through the streets.

To show them, Helen filled a glass with water, marked the level with a pen and dropped in a handful of coins. The water rose. "Displacement," she said, and Lily repeated the word with great respect.

Then it was my turn. I am not a physicist, but I am good at storytelling, which in my family is passed down like a precious ring. I told the children about summer in my grandmother's village in Ireland, where people still lit fires on the hills on the shortest night of the year. The custom goes back to pagan times, long before the first churches were built, when the pagan festival celebrated the sun at its strongest.

My grandmother was a practical woman, but she had a mystic side. She believed that the smoke of the summer fire brought luck to the fields, and she walked her children through it every year. She was not really a mystic, I told Owen and Lily; she simply loved a good story. Still, by the light of the candles, with the wind outside, even Helen admitted that a little mystic feeling was hard to avoid.

Around midnight, the lights came back on. The refrigerator started up, the television woke, and the children sighed. Owen asked if we could have another blackout next week. I told him that our family was not going to become extinct after all. We had simply discovered that storytelling still works without electricity.

Questions:
Why did Owen think the family would become extinct?
He thought that without electricity the family would disappear like the dinosaurs.
What is displacement, according to Helen?
It is the rise of the water when a body pushes water out of its way.
Where does the custom of the summer fires come from?
It goes back to pagan times, before the first churches were built.
What did the family discover during the blackout?
They discovered that storytelling still works without electricity.

lessons.title: Cold Toes and Hockey
lessons.summary: A father from the desert learns to be a hockey parent and learns a lesson from his son.
lessons.text:
Until three years ago, my family lived in a small city in southwestern Arizona, where summer temperatures reach 115 degrees and the only ice is in your drink. Then my job moved us to Minnesota, and our son, Ben, who was eight at the time, discovered hockey.

In southwestern Arizona, children play soccer and baseball; hockey is something you watch on television, if at all. In Minnesota, however, hockey is less a sport than a way of life, and Ben was a fan within a week. My mother, back in Arizona, sent dire warnings about broken teeth. Her warnings became more dire with every photo of Ben in his helmet.

The first thing I learned as a hockey parent was that an ice arena is cold. You sit on a metal bench at six in the morning, holding a cup of coffee, and within twenty minutes your toes are numb.

The second thing I learned was how small a puck is. A puck is a hard rubber disc, black and about three inches wide, and it moves faster than my eyes can follow. For a whole season, Ben chased the puck the way a puppy chases a ball, with great energy and no results. Then one Saturday he took the puck from an opponent, skated toward the goal and shot. The puck hit the back of the net, and I jumped up and spilled coffee on a stranger.

The third lesson was harder, and it was about me. In hockey, a player who argues with the referee or behaves badly can be given a misconduct penalty and sent off the ice for ten minutes. The coaches told the boys to respect the referees, and the boys mostly did. The parents were another matter. The prevalence of shouting among hockey parents is so high that many arenas now put up signs reminding adults to behave. I was not immune. One morning, after a call that I thought was wrong, I heard myself shouting at a referee who was perhaps sixteen years old.

On the drive home, Ben was quiet. Then he said, "Dad, if I did that, I'd get a misconduct." He was right. It was hypocrisy to teach him to respect referees and then shout at one myself, and I told him so. Children notice hypocrisy faster than anything else, and luckily they forgive it faster than we deserve.

Since then, I keep my mouth shut and my coffee in both hands. Last week, Ben's team lost 5 to 2. Afterward he shook the referee's hand, as the players always do, and then he skated to the glass where I was sitting and knocked on it with his glove. I knocked back. My toes were numb and my coffee was cold, but I could not have been happier.

Questions:
What does the writer say about the prevalence of shouting?
The prevalence of shouting among hockey parents is so high that many arenas put up signs.
What is a puck?
A puck is a hard rubber disc, black and about three inches wide.
What is a misconduct penalty?
It is a penalty for arguing with the referee or behaving badly, and the player is sent off the ice for ten minutes.
Why did Ben's father admit to hypocrisy?
He taught Ben to respect referees but then shouted at one himself.
